newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean "boat people" report starvation deaths.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean "boat people" report starvation deaths.

text.p: The first "boat people" defectors from North Korea on Thursday described people starving to death in their homeland, and said the country had been gripped by rumours of impending war against the South.

Fourteen members of two families, who created a sensation last week by becoming the first northerners to flee to the South directly by sea, told their first news conference that life in the North was a constant battle to survive.

"I had to struggle to feed five family members, and my parents had malnutrition from eating only flour porridge," said Kim Hwa-ok, 41, the wife of the vessel's captain, who arrived with their three children and his mother.
"In April and May, I saw two people who had died of starvation," she said.
The other family included the ship's engineer, Kim Won-hyung, his wife and their four children, a daughter-in-law and two-year-old grandson.

The engineer said rumours were spreading that North Korean leader Kim Jung-il would launch an attack on the South between July and October at the end of a three-year mourning period for his father, the late "great leader" Kim Il-sung.
Separately, the son of the 57-year-old engineer was quoted as telling intelligence authorities that North Korea was mobilising for war.

"Despite severe food shortages, North Korea recently extended enlisted service for soldiers in the people's armed forces," a statement by the Agency for National Security Planning quoted him as saying.
"It has also begun to draft even those teenagers of non-communist and non-proletarian backgrounds, previously excluded from the military service, to strengthen the North's fighting force."
Nurses and doctors were being trained in wartime medicine, another of the defectors was quoted as saying.

South Koreans are already alarmed by reports from the highest-level North Korean ever to defect that the hunger-stricken Stalinist nation could "scorch" South Korea and Japan with nuclear weapons and was preparing for conflict.
Hwang Jang-yop, Pyongyang's former top ideologue, arrived last month after fleeing through Beijing and Manila.

In the latest defection, the captain of the 32-tonne wooden fishing vessel set sail from the river port of Shinuiju near the northern border with China and picked up other passengers further down the coast.
The defectors all looked healthy, and although some of the children seemed short they were plump and with good complexions.
The engineer's son said no international food aid appeared to have reached civilians in Shinuiju.

"I don't know why they are even sending the aid when no civilians in Shinuiju seem to be receiving it," said Kim Hee-sung, 20. "Some say it is going to the military. They might as well not send food aid."

The boat was bought in China using $20,000 given to the engineer by his twin brother living in the United States. It was loaded with sacks of rice and corn when it was intercepted by the South Korean navy on Monday last week.
Both the captain and engineer had privileged positions in North Korea, where they were entrusted with earning foreign exchange and given unusual freedom to travel.
Engineer Kim said his family led a comfortable life in the North despite looming famine.
